row.basis: first litigant and counter-questioning
row.note: The commentary opens with both sides claiming haqq; this proverb says the first litigant seems right until the other examines the case, making reciprocal hearing the test of a claim.

row.basis: truth to neighbor; judgments of peace
row.note: The commentary turns haqq from a contested possession into something exchanged; Zechariah joins speaking truth to one's neighbor with judgments of truth and peace in the city gate.

row.basis: burdens and disputes not borne alone
row.note: Moses says he cannot bear the people's troubles, burdens, and disputes alone; the commentary likewise moves from the solitary human in loss to mutual counsel.

row.basis: wise people appointed to judge
row.note: After naming the people's disputes as too much for one person, Moses asks them to select wise and discerning leaders; this distributes the work of judging competing claims.

row.basis: Moses unable to carry the people alone
row.note: Moses says the people's burden is too heavy for him alone; this gives a concrete counterpart to the commentary's solitary human in loss before its turn toward shared support.

row.basis: elders share Moses's burden
row.note: God puts some of Moses's spirit on the elders so they bear the people with him; the scene makes the commentary's move from lone loss to a group that carries together concrete.

row.basis: strife stopped because the parties are kin
row.note: Abram asks that there be no strife between him and Lot because they are brothers; kinship removes the repulsion that the commentary says sulh repairs.

row.basis: Ruth binds herself to Naomi and her people
row.note: As bereaved Naomi urges Ruth to leave, Ruth joins her fate, people, and God to Naomi's; this turns loss into chosen kinship and answers the solitary-human image.

row.basis: reproof of a fellow without hatred
row.note: The command to reprove one's fellow rather than harbor hatred makes correction a duty within a relationship, close to the commentary's reciprocal counsel.

row.basis: one raises a fallen companion
row.note: Ecclesiastes calls the solitary fallen person wretched because no one is there to lift him; the companion's action directly answers the commentary's human alone in loss.

row.basis: one person sharpens another
row.note: The proverb makes reciprocal influence the means by which a person is sharpened; the commentary likewise stresses that each gives and receives in mutual counsel.

row.basis: disputants heard and judged
row.note: When two people have a dispute, judges decide between them and distinguish the righteous from the guilty; this locates contested right in a hearing rather than either side's assertion alone.

row.basis: Esau embraces the brother he had opposed
row.note: Esau runs to Jacob, embraces him, and they weep; the estranged brothers' bodily welcome gives a particular scene of hostility yielding to closeness.

row.basis: captured enemies fed and released
row.note: Elisha has the Aramean captives fed before they return home, after which their raiding bands stop; hospitality changes the enemy relation that the commentary says peace can transform.

row.basis: captives treated as kin and returned
row.note: Israelite leaders clothe, feed, and transport Judean captives back to their kin; care across a hostile conflict makes the commentary's removal of estrangement tangible.

row.basis: two kingdoms made one people
row.note: Ezekiel says divided Israel and Judah will no longer be two nations but one under one king; this pictures separated groups joined into one community.

row.basis: faithfulness meets truth; peace kisses righteousness
row.note: The psalm personifies truth and peace as meeting partners; this closely joins the commentary's contested haqq to peace and a bond between people.

row.basis: those who fear God speak to one another
row.note: Their shared speech is heard and remembered by God; the verse gives the commentary's mutual exchange a communal act with divine recognition.

row.basis: friend's earnest counsel gladdens the heart
row.note: The proverb locates a friend's sweetness in earnest counsel; the commentary's close friend and reciprocal advice meet in one concrete relation.

row.basis: companion to all who keep God's precepts
row.note: The speaker calls himself companion to all who fear God and keep the commandments; this gives the commentary's intimacy an ethical, shared-practice basis.

row.basis: friends remain beside Job in grief
row.note: Job's friends sit with him on the ground for seven days without speaking; their patient presence fits the commentary's companion standing beside a group and answers isolation through company.

row.basis: God makes even enemies live at peace
row.note: The proverb says a person's God-pleasing ways can bring enemies to peace; it directly develops the commentary's movement from hostility toward friendly relation.

row.basis: Egypt, Assyria, and Israel share a blessing
row.note: The prophet names former rival peoples together as God's people, handiwork, and inheritance; this extends the commentary's turn from hostility to kin-like belonging across nations.

row.basis: brothers dwelling together in unity
row.note: The psalm calls brothers' shared dwelling good and pleasant; it gives a compact image of the communal closeness set against the commentary's isolated human.

row.basis: a friend closer than a brother
row.note: The proverb distinguishes ordinary companions from a friend who stays closer than kin; it concretizes the commentary's gloss of a chosen, intimate friend.

row.basis: Daniel brings his companions into the crisis
row.note: Daniel tells Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah what threatens him and asks them to seek mercy together; shared appeal replaces the impossible task facing a human alone.

row.basis: Hebrew אנוש, mortal human in trouble
row.note: The commentary labels الإنسان under ء ن س; the table notes BDB's Arabic-cognate note for Hebrew אנוש, and Job describes this mortal human as short-lived and full of trouble, sharpening the ayah's human-in-loss claim.

row.basis: Hebrew אנוש, mortal whom God remembers
row.note: The commentary labels الإنسان under ء ن س; the table notes BDB's Arabic-cognate note for אנוש, and this psalm asks why God remembers the mortal, adding divine regard to the ayah's exposed human.

row.basis: Aaron loves peace and brings people near Torah
row.note: The Mishnah interprets peacemaking as active pursuit joined to love of people and drawing them near; it expands the commentary's sulh from ending repulsion to restoring closeness.

row.basis: Aaron reconciles two disputants through personal messages
row.note: The tradition depicts Aaron telling each disputant that the other regrets the quarrel until they meet and embrace; it turns the commentary's mutual counsel into a specific practice of restoring bonds.

row.basis: stay with the community; do not judge before knowing one's place
row.note: The Mishnah warns against separation from the community and premature judgment of another; this answers the commentary's isolated human and the disputants each sure of their own right.

row.basis: Hillel's school presents Shammai's view before its own
row.note: The schools' dispute remains a shared search, and Hillel's humility and fair teaching explain why his view prevails; this gives the commentary's opposing claims a model of argument that preserves relationship.

row.basis: jesters cheer the sad and reconcile quarrelers
row.note: The two men describe both lifting the downcast and making peace between disputants; their paired actions join companionship in loss to active reconciliation.

row.basis: Israel responsible for one another
row.note: The dictum that all Israel are guarantors for one another states the mutual obligation implicit when the commentary says each gives and receives counsel.

row.basis: wisdom comes from learning from every person
row.note: Ben Zoma defines the wise person as one who learns from everyone; this makes the commentary's reciprocal relation a source of wisdom rather than solitary possession.

row.basis: disputes for Heaven's sake endure
row.note: The Mishnah contrasts enduring disputes for Heaven, exemplified by Hillel and Shammai, with a dispute that does not endure; it distinguishes principled disagreement from contention that destroys bonds.

row.basis: peace between people as a deed with lasting fruit
row.note: The Mishnah explicitly lists making peace between one person and another among deeds whose fruit is enjoyed in this world; it links the commentary's good action to repaired relations.

row.basis: bringing peace between a person and a fellow
row.note: The Talmud names interpersonal peacemaking among deeds rewarded in this world; this gives the commentary's sulh a concrete ethical practice.

row.basis: neighbor-love as a great principle of Torah
row.note: Rabbi Akiva reads love of one's neighbor as a great principle; this interpretation makes the commentary's intimacy and mutual care a frame for the wider law.

row.basis: reconcile disputants, judge rightly, reprove without partiality
row.note: The teaching rejects division, orders reconciliation and fair judgment, then forbids partiality in reproof; it closely joins the commentary's peace, haqq, and mutual counsel.

row.basis: reconcile with a brother before offering a gift
row.note: Jesus makes repair with an estranged brother prior to altar worship; the scene gives social reconciliation priority over a religious act.

row.basis: settle quickly with an accuser on the way to court
row.note: The instruction to reach agreement with one's legal opponent before judgment directly meets the commentary's opening image of parties asserting their own right.

row.basis: private correction aims to regain a brother
row.note: The offended person is to speak directly and, if heard, has gained a brother; this makes admonition a means of restoring kinship rather than winning a case.

row.basis: dispute and debate over circumcision
row.note: The believers' serious dispute over Gentile inclusion gives the commentary's contested claims a concrete communal case rather than a generic quarrel.

row.basis: communal decision reached with the Spirit and the assembly
row.note: The council says its decision seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them together; this gives the preceding dispute a shared, non-solitary resolution.

row.basis: welcome the dissenter without quarrelling over opinions
row.note: Paul instructs the community to receive the person with a different food practice without turning opinions into a fight; this answers the commentary's move from claims to belonging.

row.basis: eater and abstainer must not despise or judge
row.note: Paul names both sides of the practice dispute and says God has welcomed each; this directly checks mutual claims of moral superiority.

row.basis: pursue peace and mutual upbuilding
row.note: Paul joins the pursuit of peace to building one another up; this closely matches the commentary's reciprocal movement from contested truth to mutual counsel.

row.basis: accepting wrong instead of litigating with a brother
row.note: The commentary turns haqq into truth passed mutually, while Paul says that lawsuits among believers are already defeat and asks why they do not accept being wronged; the differing remedy is the point.

row.basis: Christ makes two groups one by breaking hostility
row.note: The letter pictures peace as removing the dividing wall between groups; this gives the commentary's sulh a concrete image of estrangement dismantled.

row.basis: patience bears with one another in love
row.note: The community is told to practice humility, patience, and forbearance toward one another; this connects the commentary's ṣabr to sustaining relationship.

row.basis: unity held by the bond of peace
row.note: The letter describes peace as the bond that preserves communal unity; this closely meets the commentary's movement from aversion to attachment.

row.basis: speak truth to neighbor because members belong to one another
row.note: Paul joins truthful speech to mutual membership in one body; this directly links the commentary's haqq with its hand-to-hand relation.

row.basis: restore the transgressor gently
row.note: Paul says to restore a caught person in a spirit of gentleness while watching oneself; correction becomes mutual care rather than adversarial judgment.

row.basis: bear one another's burdens
row.note: The command to carry one another's burdens makes the commentary's move from the solitary human to companions who stand together concrete.

row.basis: admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
row.note: The community is to give different forms of support to the idle, fainthearted, and weak, then remain patient with everyone; this is reciprocal counsel enacted as care.

row.basis: consider one another and stir up love and good works
row.note: The letter makes attention to others the source of mutual encouragement toward good deeds, closely joining the commentary's work and reciprocal advice.

row.basis: encourage one another as the day approaches
row.note: The command to encourage each other makes perseverance communal, matching the commentary's counsel of patience passed between people.

row.basis: righteousness is sown in peace by peacemakers
row.note: James makes peace the soil and peacemakers the agents of a harvest of righteousness; this directly joins the commentary's haqq and sulh.

row.basis: unity, sympathy, brotherly love, and humility
row.note: Peter places one-mindedness and brotherly compassion together; this gives the commentary's move from estrangement to intimacy a compact communal ethic.

row.basis: seek peace and pursue it
row.note: The letter commands active pursuit of peace, matching the commentary's account of peace as removing recoil and separation.

row.basis: feed and give drink to an enemy
row.note: Paul prescribes care for an enemy in need; this is a concrete act by which the commentary's enemy-to-close-friend movement can begin.

row.basis: overcome evil with good
row.note: Paul's concluding principle explains how good action can change the relation to an enemy, adding an ethical mechanism to the commentary's transformation.

row.basis: members care equally, without division
row.note: Paul's body image rejects division and makes members care for one another; it pictures mutual attachment as protection against isolation.

row.basis: one member's suffering is shared by all
row.note: The body's members suffer and rejoice together; this turns the commentary's human-in-loss image into shared rather than solitary experience.

row.basis: bear with and forgive one another
row.note: The instruction makes forbearance and forgiveness reciprocal; it shows patience operating directly between people.

row.basis: love binds everything together
row.note: Love is named the bond that brings the virtues to completion; this adds a binding image to the commentary's account of people joining one another.

row.basis: peace of Christ rules in one body
row.note: The one body is to be governed by peace; this links reconciliation with the communal unity developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Jesus calls disciples friends and shares what he heard
row.note: The disciples are friends because Jesus has made known what he heard; this connects the commentary's intimate friend with counsel and disclosure.

row.basis: receive Onesimus as a beloved brother
row.note: Paul asks Philemon to receive the formerly enslaved Onesimus no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother; the appeal turns hierarchy and estrangement toward kinship.

row.basis: restore, encourage, agree, and live in peace
row.note: Paul joins restoration and mutual encouragement to agreement and peace, closely matching the commentary's sequence from conflict to togetherness.

row.basis: one person gives way so the community may live in peace
row.note: Clement asks anyone causing strife to leave voluntarily if needed so the flock can live peacefully; this gives the commentary's peace a costly communal practice.

row.basis: gentle answer turns away anger
row.note: The commentary says peace removes repulsion; Proverbs identifies a gentle reply as one way to turn wrath aside, though it describes one speaker's action rather than reciprocal counsel.

row.basis: seek peace and pursue it
row.note: The psalm's active pursuit of peace fits the commentary's repair of separation; its general exhortation leaves the parties and process unspecified.

row.basis: close companion becomes the speaker's betrayer
row.note: The commentary glosses intimacy as a close friend; the psalm recalls a familiar companion who shared counsel but became an adversary, preserving the contrary possibility that closeness can rupture.

row.basis: Moses speaks with God as with a friend
row.note: The commentary develops the close-friend sense of its insan word-family; Exodus uses friendship for face-to-face intimacy, an analogue that is explicitly divine-human rather than between peers.

row.basis: a shared cord resists being broken
row.note: Ecclesiastes says two withstand attack and a threefold cord is not quickly torn; this pictures the resilience of joined people, extending the commentary's bond image beyond counsel.

row.basis: Hebrew חקק and ḥuqqim, prescribed statutes
row.note: The commentary labels haqq under ح ق ق and says it passes between people; the table offers Hebrew חקק as an unverified sound correspondence, and the child's question about statutes begins an intergenerational transmission of prescribed teaching rather than a litigant's claim.

row.basis: no human on earth can answer the king
row.note: The commentary labels الإنسان under ء ن س and places the human in loss; the Aramaic verse says no human can meet the impossible demand, then Daniel turns to companions, making the following shared appeal a pointed contrast.

row.basis: Aramaic אנש, human unable to answer alone
row.note: The commentary labels الإنسان under ء ن س; the table lists Aramaic אנש only as an unverified sound correspondence, and this verse uses it for a human no one on earth can find capable of the task.

row.basis: Hebrew אנוש, mortal whom God remembers
row.note: The commentary's source label for الإنسان is ء ن س; the table notes BDB's Arabic-cognate note for אנוש, while the psalm contrasts human smallness with God's remembering and honor.

row.basis: Hebrew אנוש, mortal and troubled
row.note: The commentary's source label for الإنسان is ء ن س; the table notes BDB's Arabic-cognate note for אנוש, and Job's short-lived, trouble-filled mortal gives a specific Hebrew use of the human-in-loss image.

row.basis: עצרת, a gathered festival assembly
row.note: The commentary glosses its Arabic root label ع ص ر as a bond of affection or kinship; the table gives Hebrew עצר as a sound correspondence, and Deuteronomy's ʿăṣārâ names a public assembly, a related gathering image with a distinct sense.

row.basis: justice, truth, and peace sustain the world
row.note: The Mishnah places justice, truth, and peace together as the world's supports; this gives a compact ethical frame for the commentary's claims of haqq, peace, and communal relation.

row.basis: scholars increase peace in the world
row.note: The Talmud reads the scriptural promise of peace through the work of scholars; this links the commentary's mutual counsel to peace-making, though by an interpretive bridge.

row.basis: rebuke a brother who sins
row.note: Jesus commands attention to a brother's wrongdoing; with the following forgiveness instruction, correction serves the relationship rather than a contest over right.

row.basis: forgive a repentant brother repeatedly
row.note: Jesus says to forgive the same brother even after repeated offenses if he repents; this makes patience a repeated practice sustaining kinship.

row.basis: regard others with humility
row.note: Paul's instruction to count others above oneself counters each party's insistence that haqq belongs to it, though it frames humility rather than mutual truth-telling.

row.basis: live peaceably with everyone as far as possible
row.note: Paul makes peace an active communal aim while acknowledging limits; this fits the commentary's removal of estrangement without specifying a single dispute.

row.basis: walking in light yields fellowship with one another
row.note: The letter joins shared truthfulness before God to fellowship among believers; this connects the commentary's haqq with its movement toward closeness.

row.basis: division tears the community as Christ's body
row.note: Clement condemns strife as tearing apart members of one body; this makes communal loss the consequence of the division the commentary seeks to overcome.

row.basis: ʿăṣārâ, assembly; table sound correspondence only
row.note: The commentary's gloss of Arabic ع ص ر concerns absent affection or kinship, while this Hebrew form means a festival assembly; the possible link is only the shared gathering image, not an established shared sense.

row.basis: neighbor-love instead of vengeance or grudge
row.note: The verse forbids vengeance and resentment between members of the people before commanding love of neighbor; it gives the commentary's move from conflict to closeness a concrete ethical form.

row.basis: true judgments joined to kindness and mercy
row.note: Zechariah tells the community to judge truthfully and show compassion to one another; this adds mercy to the commentary's link between haqq and peace.

row.basis: do not scheme evil against one another
row.note: The verse forbids plotting harm against a neighbor and loving false oaths; it continues the preceding truth-and-peace formula with an explicit interpersonal restraint.

row.basis: one Father and treachery between brothers
row.note: Malachi asks why people betray one another if they share one creator and ancestral covenant; this grounds the commentary's kinship bond in a moral claim against division.

row.basis: wise person listens to counsel
row.note: The fool thinks his way right in his own eyes, but the wise listen to counsel; this directly answers the commentary's image of each side claiming haqq for itself.

row.basis: slow anger calms contention
row.note: The patient person quiets a quarrel, while the hot-tempered one stirs it; this gives sabr a direct social effect in ending strife.

row.basis: repeating an offense separates close friends
row.note: The proverb says covering a transgression seeks love while repeating it divides intimate friends; it makes the commentary's friend-bond vulnerable to speech that renews conflict.

row.basis: feed an enemy who is hungry
row.note: The proverb commands concrete care for an enemy in need; it gives an action by which the commentary's transition from enmity toward friendship can begin.

row.basis: faithful wounds from a friend
row.note: The proverb treats a friend's painful rebuke as faithful; it clarifies that the commentary's mutual advice can correct rather than merely affirm a companion.

row.basis: peace offered but met with war
row.note: The speaker says he is for peace while those around him want war; this preserves a counter-case to the commentary's hopeful passage from mutual speech to peace.

row.basis: peace wished for brothers and companions
row.note: The pilgrim's formula wishes peace within Jerusalem for the sake of brothers and companions; it joins liturgical speech, friendship, and communal peace in one line.

row.basis: brothers and acquaintances estranged from Job
row.note: Job says his kin have withdrawn and his acquaintances are strangers; this gives a stark counter-image to the commentary's claim that human loss is answered by bonds.

row.basis: intimate friends turn against Job
row.note: Job says those he loved have turned against him; this preserves the contrary reading that close friendship can collapse into aversion.

row.basis: Joseph tells frightened brothers not to grieve over their betrayal
row.note: Joseph reframes their sale of him as God's means of preserving life; the speech releases his brothers from fear and turns a contested wrong toward reconciliation.

row.basis: Joseph comforts his brothers and speaks kindly
row.note: After the brothers fear revenge again, Joseph reassures and comforts them; this is a necessary continuation showing reconciliation maintained through compassionate speech.

row.basis: Abigail's counsel keeps David from bloodguilt
row.note: David blesses Abigail for restraining him from revenge; her wise intervention makes counsel the means by which a violent conflict is prevented.

row.basis: elders advise the king to serve and answer gently
row.note: The elders tell Rehoboam that serving the people and speaking good words will win their service; this makes reciprocal regard a practical alternative to coercive rule.

row.basis: rejected counsel ends in the people's division
row.note: After Rehoboam rejects the elders' advice, Israel refuses his rule and separates; this shows the social loss that follows counsel answered with hardness.

row.basis: people speak to one another to build together
row.note: The repeated mutual speech coordinates Babel's brickmaking; unlike the commentary's counsel toward haqq, this is a counter-example of solidarity directed toward a self-exalting project.

row.basis: shared speech is confused so people cannot understand one another
row.note: The Babel scene reverses the commentary's image of people passing counsel between them: collective speech becomes unintelligible and the group is broken apart.

row.basis: one human ancestor taught as a basis for peace among creatures
row.note: The Mishnah says humanity descends from one person so no one can claim a superior ancestry; this directly counters rival claims and grounds common human dignity in kinship.

row.basis: divine presence rests where two discuss Torah
row.note: The Mishnah makes shared study a sacred meeting between people; it gives the commentary's reciprocal counsel a setting in which relationship itself matters.

row.basis: the neighbor treated by the golden rule
row.note: Hillel summarizes Torah through the instruction not to do to another what one hates; this makes mutual regard the test for how one treats a fellow.

row.basis: Hillel and Shammai preserve marriages despite legal disagreement
row.note: The schools disagree about rulings yet do not refuse intermarriage; this shows opposing claims coexisting without severing kinship.

row.basis: baseless hatred brings the Second Temple's destruction
row.note: The Talmud explains a communal catastrophe through hatred among people; this makes estrangement itself a source of collective loss.

row.basis: a faithful friend is a sturdy shelter and a treasure
row.note: Ben Sira gives the close friend a protective role; this concretizes the commentary's intimate bond as refuge in human vulnerability.

row.basis: forgive a neighbor before praying for forgiveness
row.note: Ben Sira makes forgiveness of another the condition mirrored in one's own prayer; this gives the commentary's repair of hostility a reciprocal religious practice.

row.basis: avoid strife because anger kindles it
row.note: The sage says restraint from quarrel reduces sin and a hot-tempered person ignites conflict; this closely joins patience with the prevention of strife.

row.basis: be at peace with one another after rivalry
row.note: After the disciples argue over greatness and dispute who belongs with them, Jesus tells them to have salt and be at peace with one another; the instruction answers internal rivalry directly.

row.basis: correct yourself before correcting your brother
row.note: Jesus requires removing one's own plank before helping a brother with his speck; this checks mutual claims of right with self-examination before advice.

row.basis: forgive a brother repeatedly
row.note: Jesus tells Peter to forgive not a few times but repeatedly; this extends the commentary's patience into sustained repair after recurring offense.

row.basis: one heart and soul with possessions shared
row.note: The believers hold themselves as one community and treat possessions as common; this gives the commentary's people-joining image a material practice.

row.basis: Barnabas introduces feared Saul to the apostles
row.note: When the disciples fear Saul, Barnabas stands with him and vouches for his changed life; an intermediary turns aversion into acceptance.

row.basis: mutual affection and honoring one another
row.note: Paul commands familial affection and outdoing one another in honor; this is a direct ethic of reciprocal closeness.

row.basis: welcome one another as Christ welcomed you
row.note: The community's welcome is grounded in the welcome it has received; this makes inclusion reciprocal rather than a claim held by one side.

row.basis: love is patient and kind
row.note: Paul makes patience and kindness qualities of love between people; this gives the commentary's ṣabr a relational rather than solitary form.

row.basis: love rejoices with the truth
row.note: Paul joins truth with love's response; this directly meets the commentary's shift from haqq as a contested claim to a shared good.

row.basis: truth spoken in love grows the body
row.note: The letter links truth-telling to love and the growth of the whole body; this adds a communal result to the commentary's exchange of haqq.

row.basis: Euodia and Syntyche urged to agree in the Lord
row.note: Paul names two women who labored in the gospel and asks them to reach agreement; the personal appeal makes counsel address an actual community conflict.

row.basis: a companion asked to help the women reconcile
row.note: Paul asks a trusted coworker to assist the women who struggled beside him; the continuation makes reconciliation a shared responsibility.

row.basis: the Lord's servant must not quarrel but be patient
row.note: The teacher is to avoid strife, remain gentle, and endure patiently; this directly links sabr to how one handles opponents.

row.basis: correct opponents with gentleness
row.note: Correction is to be offered gently even to those who oppose; this gives mutual counsel a manner aimed at restoration rather than victory.

row.basis: love covers many sins
row.note: Peter says sustained love covers many sins; this fits the commentary's transition from contention toward a bond that can absorb offense.

row.basis: claiming love for God while hating a brother is false
row.note: The letter tests religious claim against treatment of the visible brother; this challenges any haqq claim detached from mutual care.

row.basis: reconcile with an opponent before the communal meal
row.note: The Didache bars someone at odds with a fellow from joining the Eucharist until reconciliation; this gives the commentary's peace a concrete liturgical consequence.

row.basis: love acts in harmony and creates no schism
row.note: Clement describes love as refusing division and doing everything in harmony; this is a Christian interpretive expansion of the bond that the commentary sees replacing estrangement.

row.basis: love and guard the brother as one's own soul
row.note: The saying treats the brother's life as one's own to protect; it gives the commentary's close-friend image an unusually intimate ethical measure.

row.basis: patience persuades and a gentle tongue prevails
row.note: The proverb joins patience and gentle speech in persuading a ruler; it adds a specific way counsel can change a hard position without quarrel.

row.basis: righteousness produces peace and quiet security
row.note: Isaiah presents peace and settled confidence as the effect of righteousness; this joins ethical rightness to social calm, though it does not describe a specific dispute.

row.basis: Jerusalem destroyed for insisting on strict law
row.note: The Talmud interprets the city's destruction as a failure to go beyond the letter of law; this provides a Jewish counter-reading in which claiming formal right without generosity cannot sustain peace.

row.basis: a faithful friend is life-saving medicine
row.note: The friend is described as healing support found by those who fear God; this adds the companion's restorative effect to the commentary's account of connection.
